name: Food truck business
blurb: Sell food from a licensed truck or trailer at events, markets and busy street spots
title: Food Truck Business: How to Start, Permits and Risks
description: How to start a food truck: how it makes money, the vehicle, permits and kitchen rules to check, who it suits, the main risks and how to test your menu first.
h1: How to start a food truck
answer: A food truck business sells a short menu from a licensed truck or trailer at street spots, markets, offices and private events. It costs less than a restaurant but still needs a vehicle, kitchen equipment and several permits, and long hours, breakdowns and rules about where you can park are what wear most owners down.

sections.h: How a food truck makes money
body: Customers pay per item or meal. Many trucks also earn from catering private events, weddings and office lunches, where the income is booked in advance and more predictable.

Costs include ingredients, packaging, fuel, propane, commissary kitchen fees where required, event or pitch fees, payment fees, insurance, repairs and staff. Waste from unsold food eats margin quickly.

ul: A truck or trailer fitted to local health and fire standards; used ones need inspecting before you buy.
Permits: rules differ by country and city. Examples include a business licence, a mobile food vendor permit, food handler certificates, health inspection and fire safety checks.
Access to an approved kitchen or commissary if your area requires one for prep and storage.
A short, fast menu you can cook well in a small space, and a way to tell people where you will be.

sections.h: Who it suits (and who it doesn't)

head: Suits
Not for
rows: Cooks who want to test a concept before a restaurant
People comfortable with driving, setup and long days
People who dislike paperwork and inspections
Areas with markets, events and office lunch crowds
Cities that heavily restrict where trucks can park

ul: Parking and zoning rules can limit where and when you trade.
Breakdowns and equipment failures cost both repairs and lost days.
Weather and seasons: outdoor trade can drop sharply in rain, cold or heat.
Used truck sales: check the kitchen, gas lines and vehicle condition before you pay.
Long hours beyond service time: prep, cleaning, driving and admin.

sections.h: How to test it cheaply first

ol: Cook your menu for friends and record how long each dish takes.
Run a stall at a local market or event using a rented setup if allowed.
Ask your city or council exactly which permits a mobile food business needs.
Visit busy truck spots and note prices, queues and how many trucks compete.
Get quotes for a used truck, fit-out and insurance before deciding.
Get the permits, inspections and insurance in place before your first service.
Fix a short menu and cost every dish, including packaging.
Book a few markets or events and one regular weekly spot.
Post your schedule where customers will see it each week.
Track sales, waste and hours by location, and drop spots that do not pay.

faq.q: Is a food truck cheaper than a restaurant?
faq.a: Usually, because there is no shop lease or full fit-out, but the truck, kitchen equipment and permits are still a large cost. Get local quotes before assuming it is cheap.

faq.q: What permits does a food truck need?
faq.a: It depends on your city and country. Common examples are a business licence, a mobile vendor permit, food handler certificates, health and fire inspections, and sometimes a commissary kitchen. Ask your local authority.

faq.q: Should I rent or buy a food truck?
faq.a: Renting or sharing a truck lets you test the menu and spots before committing. Buy once you know where you will trade and what equipment you need.
